$comment: Intrvue.ai Medicine — current-affairs register. Tier 1 = evergreen NHS/healthcare knowledge. Tier 2 = slowly changing policy. Tier 3 = fast-moving. Every Tier 3 entry has a hard expiry_date; past expiry the topic is WITHHELD from users, not merely flagged. The template at the top is the contract for adding new topics without touching the system.
verified_by: Primary-source research 29 August 2026. Government change independently confirmed against gov.uk: Andy Burnham became Prime Minister 20 July 2026; Yvette Cooper appointed Secretary of State for Health and Social Care 20 July 2026.

template.title: Short topic name
template.baseline_knowledge: What an applicant is expected to be able to say. Three to five bullets maximum. If it takes more, the topic is too broad and should be split.
template.not_required: What they explicitly do NOT need to know. This field prevents scope creep and stops the scorer penalising absent detail.
stakeholders: Who has an interest and what they want
central_tensions: The unresolved conflicts. If a topic has no tension it is not an interview topic, it is a fact.
ethical_principles: Which principles are actually in play — never all four by default
likely_questions: Phrased as an interviewer would ask them
weak_answer_patterns: Specific failure modes, used to generate feedback
balanced_answer_components: What a strong answer contains. Never a model answer.
source_types: The classes of source a content writer should use
template.expiry_trigger: The named event that invalidates this entry
template.current_state: Dated facts. Every figure carries its date and source. This is the ONLY field that changes on a routine refresh — everything above it is stable.

topics.title: How the NHS is structured and funded
baseline_knowledge: Funded from general taxation, free at the point of use, based on clinical need not ability to pay
Primary care as first contact and gatekeeper; secondary and tertiary care by referral
Health is devolved: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland run separate systems with different structures and targets
A finite budget means rationing is explicit rather than optional
The NHS Constitution sets out six values
topics.not_required: Budget figures, the names of arm's-length bodies, commissioning mechanics, the difference between an ICB and an ICS in detail.
central_tensions: Comprehensive versus affordable
National standards versus local variation
Free at the point of use versus rising demand
likely_questions: What are the founding principles of the NHS and are they still achievable?
What does 'free at the point of use' actually mean?
Is the NHS the same across the UK?
weak_answer_patterns: 'The NHS is free'
Describing the NHS as hospitals
Treating English policy as UK policy
Reciting the Constitution values as a list
balanced_answer_components: The principle stated with its cost consequence
An acknowledgement that finite budgets force choices
At least one concrete example of what the principle means in practice
source_types: Nuffield Trust and King's Fund explainers
topics.expiry_trigger: A change to the founding funding model
topics.current_state: Stable. Note that structural reform (CA-014) is changing the organisational layer, not the funding principle.

topics.title: What a doctor's job actually involves
baseline_knowledge: Most care is delivered by multidisciplinary teams
Much of medicine manages rather than cures
Documentation, coordination and communication occupy more time than dramatic intervention
Uncertainty is the normal working condition
topics.not_required: Specialty-specific working patterns; the detail of any clinical role.
central_tensions: Public expectation of cure versus the reality of management
Doctor as decision-maker versus doctor as team member
likely_questions: What do you think a doctor spends most of their time doing?
What is the hardest part of the job?
What does the doctor add that another member of the team does not?
weak_answer_patterns: A cure-focused account
Elevating the doctor by diminishing other professions
Citing television
balanced_answer_components: A specific mundane element named
An account of the doctor's distinctive contribution that does not disparage others
Evidence from the candidate's own observation
source_types: MSC Role of the Doctor consensus statement
topics.current_state: Stable.

topics.title: Health inequalities: the concept
baseline_knowledge: Social determinants — housing, income, education, work, environment — drive outcomes more than healthcare does
The inverse care law: good medical care tends to vary inversely with need
Inequality appears in uptake as well as in provision
Healthcare can mitigate but not resolve inequality
topics.not_required: Specific statistics (those sit in CA-015), the Marmot review's recommendations in detail.
central_tensions: Treating illness versus preventing it
NHS responsibility versus cross-government responsibility
Universal provision versus proportionate targeting
likely_questions: Why do people in poorer areas die younger?
Whose job is it to fix health inequality?
Is the NHS making inequality better or worse?
weak_answer_patterns: Treating it as an access-to-GP problem
Naming the inverse care law with no example
Attributing outcomes to individual choices alone
balanced_answer_components: Named determinants beyond healthcare
Recognition that the NHS is downstream of the causes
One concrete mechanism, e.g. differential uptake or differential provision
topics.current_state: Concept stable. Live 2026 illustration: the Health Foundation warned on 13 August 2026 that historic underinvestment in GP funding puts the neighbourhood health agenda at risk.

topics.title: Screening: principles and harms
baseline_knowledge: Screening a healthy population differs fundamentally from testing a symptomatic one
Harms include false positives, overdiagnosis, overtreatment and anxiety
A screening programme must meet criteria about the condition, the test and the availability of treatment
More screening is not automatically better
topics.not_required: Sensitivity and specificity calculations, the full Wilson-Jungner list, programme-specific intervals.
central_tensions: Individual reassurance versus population harm
Campaigning pressure versus evidence thresholds
Early detection versus overdiagnosis
likely_questions: Should we screen everyone for cancer?
What are the downsides of a screening programme?
weak_answer_patterns: 'More screening is better'
Not distinguishing screening from diagnostic testing
Ignoring the harms entirely
balanced_answer_components: At least one named harm with a mechanism
Recognition that a test with imperfect accuracy applied to a low-prevalence population generates mostly false positives
The evidence-versus-advocacy tension
topics.expiry_trigger: A major programme change
topics.current_state: Live worked example: on 28 May 2026 the UK NSC recommended targeted prostate screening for men aged 45-61 with a confirmed BRCA2 variant and a family history, PSA every two years. BRCA1 carriers were excluded from the final version having been present in the November 2025 draft; family history alone does not qualify. Around 8 in 10 PSA positives are false. This is the cleanest available case of a committee declining population screening on evidence grounds against strong campaigning pressure.

topics.title: Antimicrobial resistance
baseline_knowledge: Resistance rises with antibiotic use, in humans and in agriculture
The UK has a national action plan with a use-reduction target
The pipeline for new antibiotics is weak because the commercial incentive is inverted — we want drugs we do not use
Restraint conflicts with access and with diagnostic uncertainty
topics.not_required: Resistance mechanisms, specific organisms, prescribing guidelines.
central_tensions: The individual patient in front of you versus the population over time
Restraint versus diagnostic uncertainty and access
Market failure versus the need for new drugs
likely_questions: Why is antimicrobial resistance a problem?
Should GPs be allowed to prescribe antibiotics on request?
How do you make a market for a drug you hope nobody needs?
weak_answer_patterns: Blaming patients as the whole answer
Not recognising the diagnostic-uncertainty pressure on prescribers
Treating it as a purely medical rather than agricultural and global problem
balanced_answer_components: The individual-versus-population tension named explicitly
Recognition that a prescriber under uncertainty faces a real cost of withholding
Awareness of the subscription payment model as an attempted fix
topics.expiry_trigger: Publication of a new national action plan (current one runs 2024-2029)
topics.current_state: 'Confronting antimicrobial resistance 2024 to 2029' is the UK's third five-year plan, published 8 May 2024, with a vision of AMR contained, controlled and mitigated by 2040. Target: reduce total human antibiotic use by 5% from a 2019 baseline by 2029. One-year progress report published 24 September 2025 reported 1.1 million fewer GP antibiotic prescriptions in England in 2023-24, a 3.2% reduction. Global context: AMR associated with roughly 4.95 million deaths annually (2019 estimate).

topics.title: Prevention versus treatment, and the regulation debate
baseline_knowledge: Prevention is cheaper and slower; its benefits are diffuse and its costs immediate, which is why it is chronically underfunded
Regulation consistently outperforms information campaigns
The 'nanny state' objection is a real argument about autonomy, not merely an obstacle
Choice is unequally available, which weakens pure individual-responsibility framings
topics.not_required: Public health grant figures, specific behavioural science models.
central_tensions: Autonomy versus population benefit
Immediate cost versus deferred benefit
Individual responsibility versus structural constraint
likely_questions: Should the government tell people what to eat?
Is a sugar tax fair?
Why does the NHS spend so little on prevention?
weak_answer_patterns: Dismissing the libertarian objection without engaging it
'We should focus on prevention' with no account of why we don't
Assuming information campaigns work
balanced_answer_components: The strongest version of the autonomy objection, stated fairly
The deprivation argument about unequal choice
The political-economy reason prevention loses to treatment
topics.expiry_trigger: Major new public health legislation
topics.current_state: Tobacco and Vapes Act 2026 received Royal Assent 29 April 2026: a rolling generational sales ban means anyone born on or after 1 January 2009 can never legally be sold tobacco; the first affected cohort turns 18 in January 2027. Vending machine ban 29 October 2026; retailer display compliance 1 January 2027; advertising ban 1 June 2027. A UK-wide consultation on plain white vape packaging opened 10 July 2026. A ban on selling high-caffeine energy drinks to under-16s was announced 16 July 2026, effective April 2027. HFSS advertising restrictions (9pm TV watershed and paid-for online) are in force. Note the Spending Review cuts non-NHS DHSC day-to-day spend by 4.5% a year, hitting the public health grant.

topics.title: Physician associates and the shape of the clinical workforce
baseline_knowledge: Physician associates are a distinct role with different training and scope, not junior doctors
The Leng Review (16 July 2025) recommended renaming, scope limits, supervision requirements and credentialling
GMC regulation began 13 December 2024 with the transition ending 13 December 2026
The debate is about scope, supervision and patient understanding — not about the individuals
topics.not_required: PA curriculum detail, headcount figures, employment terms.
central_tensions: Expanding capacity versus role clarity and safety
Professional territory versus patient benefit
Supervision requirements versus the workload of supervisors
ethical_principles: Autonomy (patients knowing who is treating them)
likely_questions: What is a physician associate?
Do you think physician associates are good for the NHS?
How should the team decide who sees which patient?
weak_answer_patterns: Not knowing what the role is
Adopting a partisan position as though it were settled
Disparaging the role or the people in it
Assuming the position is unchanged since 2024
balanced_answer_components: An accurate description of the role
Both the capacity argument and the safety argument stated fairly
Recognition that patient understanding of who is treating them is a distinct issue from competence
topics.expiry_trigger: Completion of the GMC transition on 13 December 2026, or implementation of the renaming
topics.current_state: Leng Review published 16 July 2025: rename PA to 'physician assistant' and AA to 'physician assistant in anaesthesia'; PAs should not see undifferentiated patients outside defined protocols; 2+ years secondary care before primary care; standardised badges and lanyards; named doctor supervisors; credentialling and an advanced tier. Renaming not yet fully in force as at August 2026. GMC registration becomes mandatory to use the title from 13 December 2026.

topics.title: Resource allocation, NICE and QALYs
baseline_knowledge: Funding one thing means not funding another; the unfunded alternative also has a face
NICE uses cost-per-QALY thresholds to make funding decisions explicit
Standard objections: QALYs may undervalue life with disability, discount the very old, and handle rare conditions poorly
GMP 2024 Domain 1 now includes a duty to manage resources effectively and sustainably
topics.not_required: The threshold value in pounds, NICE process detail, health economics methodology.
central_tensions: The patient in front of you versus the population
Explicit rationing versus implicit rationing
Rule-based fairness versus case-by-case compassion
likely_questions: Should the NHS fund a £300,000 drug that extends one life by six months?
Is it fair to have a price on a year of life?
Should smokers wait longer for surgery?
weak_answer_patterns: 'The NHS should fund it because it saves lives' with no counterfactual
Explaining QALYs with no critique, or rejecting them with no alternative
Dismissing desert-based arguments without engaging them
balanced_answer_components: The opportunity cost named concretely — what is displaced
The strongest objection to the mechanism proposed
Recognition that implicit rationing is worse than explicit rationing, not better
topics.expiry_trigger: A change to NICE methods
topics.current_state: Stable. Live example available via CA-016 (weight-loss medication cohorts).

topics.title: Assisted dying
baseline_knowledge: The legal position differs by jurisdiction within the British Isles and is currently moving
The core clinical arguments concern capacity assessment, prognosis reliability, coercion, conscientious objection and palliative care capacity
The constitutional argument concerns an elected chamber versus an unelected one
Assisted dying is distinct from withdrawal of treatment and from palliative sedation
topics.not_required: Clause-level bill detail, international comparisons in depth, the precise parliamentary procedure.
central_tensions: Autonomy versus protection of the vulnerable
Adequacy of palliative care as a precondition
Conscientious objection versus access
Whether safeguards can be made robust
likely_questions: Should assisted dying be legal in the UK?
What safeguards would you want to see?
Is it different from withdrawing treatment?
weak_answer_patterns: Asserting it is or is not legal without saying where
Arguing only one side
Citing the Leadbeater bill as current
Confusing it with withdrawal of treatment or with palliative sedation
balanced_answer_components: Jurisdictional accuracy
The strongest argument on each side stated fairly
At least one specific safeguard discussed with its limitation
Awareness that the position may change during the application cycle
source_types: Dignity in Dying and Care Not Killing (as advocacy, labelled as such)
topics.update_frequency: MONTHLY, and immediately after any parliamentary vote
topics.expiry_trigger: Second Reading of the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill on 11 September 2026
topics.current_state: ENGLAND AND WALES: the previous Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill passed Commons Third Reading on 20 June 2025 but ran out of time in the Lords before the session ended in May 2026 and did NOT become law; peers tabled close to 1,300 amendments. A new bill was introduced by Lauren Edwards MP on 17 June 2026 with Second Reading scheduled for FRIDAY 11 SEPTEMBER 2026. Core provisions unchanged: terminally ill, mentally competent adults with six months or less to live, two independent doctors, an expert panel, reflection periods. Campaigners argue the Parliament Act would prevent a second Lords block; this is contested. SCOTLAND: the Assisted Dying for Terminally Ill Adults (Scotland) Bill FELL at Stage 3 on 17 March 2026 (69 against, 57 for, 1 abstention). Not legal; no live bill. ISLE OF MAN: Assisted Dying Bill passed Tynwald 25 March 2025. JERSEY: States Assembly approved on 26 February 2026, 12-month prognosis for neurodegenerative conditions, expected in effect 2027. ⚠ THIS ENTRY EXPIRES 12 SEPTEMBER 2026 AND MUST BE RE-VERIFIED AFTER THE VOTE.

topics.title: Doctors' industrial action
baseline_knowledge: Who is currently in dispute and who is not
The core arguments: real-terms pay erosion versus affordability and patient harm during action
That a strike mandate can exist without strike dates
That the same doctor may hold both the patient-harm concern and the pay position
topics.not_required: Pay scale detail, DDRB process mechanics, exact ballot arithmetic.
central_tensions: The right to withdraw labour versus the duty to patients
Pay restoration as finished or paused
Short-term harm versus long-term workforce sustainability
likely_questions: Is it ever right for doctors to strike?
What would you have done during the strikes?
Whose responsibility is patient harm during industrial action?
weak_answer_patterns: Describing resident doctors as currently striking
Arguing only the patient-harm side or only the pay side
Refusing to engage on the grounds that it is political
Assuming the interviewer's sympathies
balanced_answer_components: Accurate current status
Both the professional-duty argument and the pay-erosion argument stated fairly
Recognition that the profession itself is divided
No claim to a settled answer
topics.expiry_trigger: Announcement of consultant strike dates, or expiry of the consultant mandate around July 2027
topics.current_state: The English resident doctors' dispute is OVER. On 29 June 2026 resident doctors voted to accept the government offer: 52.9% yes (17,410) to 47.1% no (15,522) on 57.3% turnout. Offer terms: average 6.6% uplift fully delivered by April 2027 (3.5% DDRB award backdated to April 2026 plus an average 3.1% over ten months); 4,000-4,500 new training posts; substantive contracts for locally employed doctors from August 2026; first two Royal College exam attempts funded from April 2026. CONSULTANTS hold a live 12-month mandate: ballot closed 6 July 2026 with 76% for action on 51.5% turnout. NO STRIKE DATES ANNOUNCED as at 29 August 2026. SAS doctors: 90% for but only 42% turnout, threshold missed. Strike days 2025: 25-30 July, 14-19 October, 17-22 December. 2026: 7-13 April, 15-19 June. Appointments and procedures lost to industrial action 2025/26: 171,776 (NHS England, May 2026). ⚠ FASTEST-MOVING ENTRY IN THE REGISTER. Consultant dates could be announced at any time. Our interviewer must never signal a position — the interviewer may be a consultant with a live mandate.

topics.title: AI in healthcare — deployment and accountability
baseline_knowledge: AI in the NHS is currently strongest in triage, documentation and image analysis, not autonomous diagnosis
Accountability does not transfer: the clinician remains responsible for decisions taken using AI
There is a regulatory line between administrative AI and clinical AI
The main risks are training-data bias, automation bias, deskilling and data governance
topics.not_required: Model architectures, specific vendor products, technical performance metrics.
central_tensions: Efficiency gains versus accountability when the tool is procured centrally and used individually
Speed of deployment versus evidence of safety
Automation reducing workload versus deskilling the workforce
Data-driven care versus consent at scale
likely_questions: Will AI replace doctors?
An AI tool recommends something you disagree with — what do you do?
If an AI gets it wrong, who is responsible?
What are the risks of AI in healthcare?
weak_answer_patterns: 'AI will/won't replace doctors' with no mechanism
Discussing AI in general rather than a named use case
Naming 'bias' with no mechanism
Not addressing accountability at all
balanced_answer_components: A named use case rather than AI in the abstract
The accountability point: responsibility stays with the clinician
A bias mechanism, e.g. under-representation in training data producing worse performance in a subgroup
Recognition that the administrative/clinical regulatory boundary is unstable as products add features
topics.expiry_trigger: A major NHS AI deployment announcement or a change to MHRA classification
topics.current_state: On 4 July 2026 NHS England announced an AI acceleration within a £10bn three-year technology and transformation programme, projected at £41bn benefit over a decade: AI triage in the NHS App (200,000+ patients within 12 months, all App users by April 2028; a trial showed a 29% reduction in GP phone queue volumes); ambient voice technology and AI notetaking in outpatients; Microsoft Copilot for 500,000+ NHS staff. On 29 July 2026 the MHRA clarified that transcription, summarisation, letter drafting and code suggestion are NOT medical devices, while ambient voice technology supporting diagnosis, treatment or prevention, or acting without clinician review, IS a regulated medical device. Clinicians remain responsible for verifying all AI outputs. The MHRA AI Airlock regulatory sandbox is in Phase 2 with £3.6m over three years. GMC position: practitioners are responsible for decisions taken using new technologies, must discuss their use with patients including uncertainties and limitations, must work within their competence, and must report adverse incidents involving software and digital tools.

topics.title: Waiting lists and elective recovery
baseline_knowledge: The 18-week referral-to-treatment standard and that the 92% constitutional standard was last met in September 2015
That the headline elective figure has improved while cancer and emergency standards have not
That improvement is unevenly distributed between trusts and regions
The distinction between pathways and patients — one person can be on several pathways
topics.not_required: Month-by-month figures, trust-level data, the RTT counting rules.
central_tensions: Headline targets versus clinical priority
Elective recovery versus emergency and cancer performance competing for the same staff
Sustainability versus hitting a milestone
likely_questions: Why are NHS waiting lists so long?
How would you reduce the waiting list?
Is hitting a target the same as improving care?
weak_answer_patterns: Citing a figure with no date
Treating the headline improvement as the whole picture
Proposing 'more funding' with no mechanism
balanced_answer_components: A dated figure
Recognition that elective, cancer and emergency performance have diverged
At least one structural cause beyond funding — workforce, flow, social care capacity
topics.expiry_trigger: Any monthly RTT publication materially changing the picture
topics.current_state: The interim 65% target was MET in March 2026: 65.3% treated within 18 weeks, waiting list down to 7.11 million pathways, the lowest in three and a half years (NHS England, 14 May 2026). The 92% constitutional standard remains the March 2029 pledge. June 2026 (BMA analysis): 7.27m pathways, roughly 6.15m patients; ~2.48m waiting over 18 weeks; ~106,000 over 52 weeks; median wait 11.9 weeks against 7.5 weeks in June 2019. A&E four-hour performance 75.4% against a 78% target (July 2026); around 47,000 twelve-hour waits for admission. Cancer: 28-day faster diagnosis 79% against 80%; 62-day 69.9% against 85%; 31-day to first treatment 92.2% against 96% (June 2026). The Health Foundation noted on 14 May 2026 that the milestone was hit while cancer and long-wait recovery targets were missed and just over 4 in 10 acute trusts failed their required improvement.

topics.title: Medical workforce, training bottleneck and international recruitment
baseline_knowledge: Competition for specialty training posts intensified sharply and legislation changed the position in 2026
A UK medical degree does not guarantee a training post
The ethical question about international medical graduates cuts both ways — fairness to UK graduates, fairness to IMGs, and the effect on source countries
The successor workforce plan is still unpublished
topics.not_required: Application ratios by specialty, immigration rules, the detail of the Act.
central_tensions: Fairness to domestic graduates versus fairness to IMGs the NHS has depended on
Domestic self-sufficiency versus global health equity
Expanding medical school places versus the training-post bottleneck downstream
likely_questions: Are there too many doctors or too few?
Is it fair to prioritise UK graduates for training posts?
What would you do if you didn't get a training post?
weak_answer_patterns: Assuming a medical degree guarantees a job
Citing pre-2026 competition ratios as current
A one-sided argument on IMGs in either direction
balanced_answer_components: Awareness that the position changed materially in 2026
Both directions of the IMG argument stated fairly
Recognition that expanding medical school places without expanding training posts moves the bottleneck rather than removing it
source_types: GMC State of Medical Education and Practice
topics.expiry_trigger: Publication of the 10 Year Workforce Plan, or the second round of post-Act recruitment
topics.current_state: The Medical Training (Prioritisation) Act 2026 received Royal Assent on 5 March 2026, prioritising UK medical graduates (plus Ireland, Iceland, Norway, Liechtenstein and Switzerland graduates, and those with British/Irish citizenship or specified immigration status) for foundation and specialty training; from 2027 the immigration-status route becomes non-automatic. NHS England reported in June 2026 that competition ratios fell from roughly 4:1 overall to about 2:1 for prioritised candidates, who filled 98% of posts (against 72% in 2025); non-prioritised applicants took 1.80% of accepted offers (against 27.95%); 100% of GP training places went to UK graduates or NHS-employed applicants. Up to 4,500 new specialty training posts over three years. The 10 Year Workforce Plan remains UNPUBLISHED, twice delayed; the 10 Year Health Plan implies FEWER staff by 2035 than the 2023 Long Term Workforce Plan projected. ⚠ Handle with care in stations — a candidate may be an international applicant or an IMG's child. Never signal a position.

topics.title: NHS structural reform
baseline_knowledge: The 10 Year Health Plan's three shifts: hospital to community, analogue to digital, treatment to prevention
NHS England is being abolished and its functions folded into the Department of Health and Social Care
Reorganisation consumes leadership capacity at the moment delivery is needed
Abolishing a layer removes a buffer but concentrates power in ministers
topics.not_required: ICB boundary detail, arm's-length body names, the legislative timetable.
central_tensions: Centralisation versus local accountability
Reform versus delivery — the same leaders cannot do both
Cost savings versus redundancy costs and lost capacity
likely_questions: What do you know about the 10 Year Health Plan?
Is abolishing NHS England a good idea?
What would you change about how the NHS is run?
weak_answer_patterns: Describing NHS England as if unchanged
Reciting the three shifts with no view on the difficulty of delivering them
Assuming reorganisation is free
balanced_answer_components: The three shifts named and one of them examined
The centralisation concern stated
Recognition that reorganisation has an opportunity cost in leadership attention
source_types: King's Fund NHS Modernisation Bill tracker
topics.expiry_trigger: Passage of the NHS Modernisation Bill, or the April 2027 'new DHSC' go-live
topics.current_state: 'Fit for the Future: 10 Year Health Plan for England' published 3 July 2025. Its legislative vehicle, the NHS Modernisation Bill, was announced in the King's Speech on 13 May 2026 and is in progress: it would abolish NHS England and fold functions into DHSC, expand Secretary of State powers over commissioning and performance, revise ICB duties, put the Single Patient Record on a statutory basis, abolish Healthwatch and merge HSSIB into the CQC. ICBs reduce from 42 to 26 via mergers effective 1 April 2026 and 1 April 2027. Around 18,000 roles to go across NHSE, DHSC and ICBs by March 2028, saving roughly £1bn a year against redundancy costs of £1bn-£1.3bn. A 'new DHSC' is targeted for April 2027. The Institute for Government found in March 2026 that ICB consolidation was 'even more problematic than anticipated'.

topics.title: Health inequality: the current numbers
baseline_knowledge: The healthy life expectancy gap between the most and least deprived areas is around two decades and has widened
Inequity shows in uptake as well as provision, with gradients by region, deprivation and ethnicity
The government's stated mission is to halve the healthy life expectancy gap between richest and poorest regions
topics.not_required: Decile-level methodology, local authority breakdowns.
central_tensions: An NHS-side policy response to socially-driven causes
Universal provision versus proportionate universalism
A stated mission versus a widening measured gap
likely_questions: How big is the health gap in this country?
Is the NHS reducing inequality?
Why do vaccination rates differ so much between areas?
weak_answer_patterns: A figure with no source or year
Explaining differential uptake as hesitancy alone
Treating the gap as static
balanced_answer_components: A dated figure with its source
Recognition that the gap has widened, not narrowed
A structural rather than attitudinal explanation for differential uptake
topics.expiry_trigger: Next ONS healthy life expectancy release
topics.current_state: ONS, 15 April 2026 (2022-2024 data), most versus least deprived decile: healthy life expectancy gap 19.3 years for males and 20.1 years for females in England (20.6 and 23.1 in Wales); life expectancy gap 10.4 years for males and 8.0 for females. In England's most deprived areas males and females expect 49.8 and 48.2 years in good health, against 69.2 and 68.5 in the least deprived — both down on 2019-2021. The deprivation HLE gap grew 22% for men and 17.1% for women between 2011-13 and 2021-23. RSV vaccination coverage in older adults at 30 June 2026 shows the uptake gradient starkly: South West 68.3% versus London 49.4%; least deprived 71.6% versus most deprived 50.3%; White British 67.0% versus Asian/Asian British-Pakistani 25.1%.

topics.title: Obesity and weight-loss medication
baseline_knowledge: The NHS is rolling out weight-loss medication in phased cohorts by BMI and comorbidity
Eligible numbers vastly exceed the numbers being treated, so rationing is explicit
The tensions are individual benefit versus population cost, medicalisation versus environment, and equity of access
BMI thresholds are adjusted for some ethnic groups because risk differs at the same BMI
topics.not_required: Drug mechanisms, side-effect profiles, dosing, trial data.
central_tensions: Treating obesity pharmacologically versus changing the food environment
Explicit cohort rationing versus need
Individual benefit versus opportunity cost at population scale
likely_questions: Should the NHS pay for weight-loss drugs?
Is obesity an individual or a societal problem?
How should the NHS decide who gets them first?
weak_answer_patterns: Treating the drugs as either a cure or a cop-out
Moralising about individual responsibility
Ignoring the opportunity cost
balanced_answer_components: Recognition that treatment and prevention are not alternatives
The rationing question addressed with a criterion
Awareness that the eligible population far exceeds capacity
topics.expiry_trigger: Move to Cohort III in 2027/28
topics.current_state: NICE TA1026 (tirzepatide); NHS England interim commissioning guidance last reviewed 2 April 2026; phased primary-care rollout began 23 June 2025. Cohort I (2025/26): BMI ≥40 with 4+ comorbidities. Cohort II (2026/27, current): BMI 35-39.9 with 4+ comorbidities. Cohort III (2027/28-2028/29): BMI ≥40 with 3+ comorbidities. BMI thresholds lowered by 2.5 kg/m² for South Asian, Chinese, other Asian, Middle Eastern, Black African and African-Caribbean groups. Approximately 220,000 people in the first three years against roughly 3.4 million fully eligible — up to 12 years to reach all of them.

topics.title: Vaccination coverage and measles
baseline_knowledge: Childhood coverage is falling and England is below the 95% threshold for MMR
Measles has caused deaths in England in 2026
The main driver is access and deprivation rather than ideological refusal
Herd immunity protects those who cannot be vaccinated, which is the collective-benefit argument
topics.not_required: Vaccine composition, schedule detail, immunology.
stakeholders: Immunosuppressed people who cannot be vaccinated
central_tensions: Parental autonomy versus collective protection
Mandates versus trust
Access barriers versus attitudinal explanations
likely_questions: Should vaccination be mandatory?
Why are vaccination rates falling?
A parent tells you they don't want their child vaccinated — what do you do?
weak_answer_patterns: Framing all non-vaccination as anti-vaccine belief
Arguing for mandates without engaging the autonomy objection
In a roleplay, lecturing rather than asking what the specific worry is
balanced_answer_components: The access-versus-attitude distinction
The collective-protection argument stated as an argument, not an assertion
In a roleplay, curiosity about the specific concern and no clinical claims
topics.expiry_trigger: Next UKHSA quarterly coverage release
topics.current_state: 736 confirmed measles cases in England from 1 January to 8 June 2026, with 106 new cases in the preceding two weeks and TWO CHILD DEATHS confirmed in 2026 (gov.uk/UKHSA, 11 June 2026). 2025 total: 959 cases. Most cases in unvaccinated children aged 10 or under; hotspots London, East of England, West Midlands. UKHSA quarterly (25 June 2026): Q1 2026 coverage at 12 months fell across the board — 6-in-1 90.1% (-0.7pp), PCV1 91.4% (-1.1pp), rotavirus 88.2% (-0.6pp), MenB 90.7% (-0.3pp); MMR1 at 24 months down 0.4pp UK and 0.5pp England. Lowest coverage in London and more deprived areas. Counter-signal: after a JCVI schedule change, second MenB dose at 6 months reached 89.8% in April 2026, up 4.6pp year on year.

topics.title: Health data, the Single Patient Record and digital exclusion
baseline_knowledge: Joined-up records improve care and create consent and trust problems at the same time
A digital front door excludes people without smartphones, connectivity, skills or English — disproportionately those who use care most
Public trust in NHS data handling is fragile and has a history
Digital exclusion is the inverse care law restated
topics.not_required: Data protection law detail, contract values, technical architecture.
central_tensions: Care improvement versus consent at scale
Opt-out convenience versus meaningful choice
Digital efficiency versus equity of access
likely_questions: Should the NHS share patient data with private companies?
What are the risks of a single patient record?
Who loses when the NHS goes digital?
weak_answer_patterns: Treating data sharing as obviously good or obviously sinister
Discussing digital transformation with no equity dimension
Confusing anonymised research data with identifiable clinical records
balanced_answer_components: The care-improvement case stated properly
The trust case stated properly, with the historical pattern acknowledged
The digital exclusion link made explicitly
topics.expiry_trigger: Passage of the NHS Modernisation Bill or a change to the Federated Data Platform contract
topics.current_state: The Single Patient Record was confirmed in the King's Speech on 13 May 2026 within the NHS Modernisation Bill, consolidating GP, hospital, specialist and social care records accessible via the NHS App, with rollout to maternity and frailty patients by 2028. The Federated Data Platform (Palantir, £330m contract, 2023) is operational and contested: reporting on 11 May 2026 indicated NHS England planned to grant Palantir and external consultancy staff admin-level access to identifiable patient data on the National Data Integration Tenant, replacing case-by-case approvals; an internal NHS briefing acknowledged 'risk of loss of public confidence'; a health minister apologised for the handling. NHS App usage, July 2026: 15.4m distinct users logged in (+26% year on year), 42.2m registered accounts, 36.8m messages delivered (+60%). The 10 Year Health Plan makes the App 'a full front door to the entire NHS by 2028'.

topics.title: Social care and its interface with the NHS
baseline_knowledge: Social care is means-tested and separately funded from the NHS, which is the root of the interface problem
Delayed discharge is a social care capacity problem presenting as a hospital problem
Reform has been repeatedly deferred
The workforce is low-paid with high turnover
topics.not_required: Funding formula detail, the history of previous reform attempts.
central_tensions: Free NHS care versus means-tested social care for the same person
Reform timetables versus present need
Pay and conditions versus local authority budgets
likely_questions: Why can't the NHS discharge patients?
Should social care be free like the NHS?
What would you do about social care?
weak_answer_patterns: Discussing NHS pressure with no reference to social care
Assuming social care is part of the NHS
Ignoring unpaid carers
balanced_answer_components: The funding-boundary explanation for delayed discharge
Recognition of the unpaid carer workforce
Awareness that reform has been deferred repeatedly and why
topics.expiry_trigger: Publication of the Casey Commission Phase 1 report
topics.current_state: The Casey Commission (launched January 2025) has NOT yet published its Phase 1 report and launched a national public engagement exercise, 'The Big Conversation on Care', on 29 July 2026; Casey warned at the LGA conference on 7 July 2026 that reform 'will fail without public consent'. On 16 July 2026 the government confirmed the first adult social care Fair Pay Agreement: an Adult Social Care Negotiating Body by end 2026, independent chair early 2027, negotiations from April 2027, first settlement April 2028, backed by £500m in 2028-29 plus £4.6bn additional adult social care funding for 2028-29, covering around 1.5 million care workers. Phase 2 of the Commission is scheduled for 2028.

topics.title: Mental health provision
baseline_knowledge: Demand for children's mental health services substantially exceeds capacity
The Mental Health Act 2025 is being commenced in stages over years, not months

Key reforms — tighter detention criteria, nominated persons, advance choice documents, removing learning disability and autism as grounds for detention — depend on workforce and resource that do not yet exist
Racial disparity in detention was a founding driver of reform and persists
topics.not_required: Section numbers, clinical pathways, diagnostic criteria.
central_tensions: Legislative reform versus the resource to deliver it
Community provision versus crisis capacity
Autonomy versus detention
likely_questions: Why are children waiting so long for mental health support?
Should mental health have parity with physical health?
What did the Mental Health Act reform change?
weak_answer_patterns: Discussing CAMHS waits with no structural explanation
Assuming the Act's reforms are already in effect
Treating parity as a slogan
balanced_answer_components: The capacity-versus-demand mechanism
Awareness that legislation is being commenced in stages
The racial disparity point where relevant
topics.expiry_trigger: Further commencement regulations under the Mental Health Act 2025
topics.current_state: The Mental Health Act 2025 received Royal Assent on 18 December 2025. First commencement 18 February 2026 (SI 2026/385). Prison-to-hospital transfer time limit expected within 18-24 months of enactment; most other changes around two years, pending a new Code of Practice and retraining; full implementation could take up to ten years. On 6 August 2026, £343m was announced for 159 new NHS mental health facilities — 100 walk-in community mental health centres (no referral needed) and 59 mental health emergency departments; first sites open autumn 2026. England currently has 6 such community centres and 23 mental health emergency departments. Over 1 million under-18s were in contact with secondary NHS mental health services in 2024-25, more than double January 2020; over 500,000 children and young people are on mental health waiting lists (BMA, July 2026).

topics.title: Private sector involvement in NHS care
baseline_knowledge: Independent providers deliver a substantial and growing share of NHS-funded elective, diagnostic and assessment work
Policy is settled in favour of routine, planned use of independent capacity
The counter-arguments concern shared workforce, casemix selection, geographic unevenness, and choice widening inequality
NHS-funded private provision is distinct from patients paying privately
topics.not_required: Contract values, provider names, procurement rules.
central_tensions: Additional throughput versus drawing on the same workforce
Lower-complexity casemix leaving trusts the complex and less remunerative work
Choice widening versus narrowing inequality
likely_questions: Should the NHS use private hospitals?
Is NHS privatisation happening?
What are the risks of using the independent sector?
weak_answer_patterns: Ideological framing in either direction with no mechanism
Confusing NHS-funded private provision with patients paying privately
Assuming private capacity is additional workforce
balanced_answer_components: The capacity argument stated properly
The shared-workforce mechanism named
The casemix and geography objections
A distinction between funding and provision
source_types: IHPN (as an interested party, labelled as such)
topics.expiry_trigger: A significant change in national policy direction
topics.current_state: The 'Elective recovery: a partnership agreement between the NHS and the independent sector' (NHS England, 6 January 2025) records the independent sector treating over 1 million NHS patients in 2024. The 10 Year Health Plan continues use of private capacity 'where it is available' and explores public-private partnerships for neighbourhood health centres. IHPN reports independent-sector diagnostics providers delivered roughly 4 million NHS scans in 2025/26, and that independent providers deliver over 50% of NHS-funded ADHD assessments (20 July 2026).

topics.title: Patient safety and the maternity investigations
baseline_knowledge: Two landmark maternity reports were published in the same week in June 2026
The recurring findings across NHS safety scandals are: women and families not listened to, fragmentation, defensiveness, and failure to act on early warnings
Candour and a learning culture are the professional response; blame is not
A statutory Maternity and Neonatal Commissioner is in prospect
topics.not_required: Case detail, clinical specifics, trust names beyond the headline.
central_tensions: Individual accountability versus systemic causes
Transparency versus defensiveness under litigation pressure
Inquiry recommendations versus implementation
likely_questions: Why do the same failures keep happening in the NHS?
How should a hospital respond when something goes wrong?
What is a learning culture?
weak_answer_patterns: Blaming individuals entirely
Using 'it's a systems issue' to avoid any accountability
Not knowing that these reports exist
balanced_answer_components: Both individual and systemic accountability held together
The 'not listened to' theme, which recurs across every inquiry
The distinction between reporting for learning and reporting for blame
topics.expiry_trigger: Government implementation of the recommendations, or a further inquiry
topics.current_state: The Ockenden final report into maternity services at Nottingham University Hospitals NHS Trust was published 24 June 2026 — the largest maternity review in NHS history, reviewing over 2,500 family cases, meeting over 500 families individually and engaging over 830 current and former staff. The National Maternity and Neonatal Investigation (Baroness Amos) published its final report on 30 June 2026, drawing on 450+ families, 10,500 public responses and 9,000 staff across 12 NHS trusts, concluding the system 'is no longer fit to consistently deliver high-quality, compassionate care', with eight recommendations headed by a statutory national Maternity and Neonatal Commissioner and themes of women not being heard, systemic racism and discrimination, and fragmentation. Government response: a statutory Commissioner, £41m additional funding, 1,000 temporary midwifery posts and a National Maternity and Neonatal Taskforce action plan.
